gaps: Every level on this page is a Yahoo Finance daily close, except the yields. Percent changes are computed from the close series shipped alongside them, never lifted from a second provider, so a level and its change always reconcile. Yields are FRED, which is the primary source for them.

Today, 11 September, is deliberately missing. Asian and commodity sessions were still open or had only just closed when this ran at 15:05 SGT. Intraday readings appear in the notes, clearly labelled, and in nothing else. An intraday level charted as a close is the single easiest way to make a dashboard lie.

The 10-year and 2-year yield series stop one session short. FRED publishes with a lag and its latest observation for both is 9 Sep. Two other readings for 10 September are quoted, attributed, in the news and instrument notes rather than spliced onto the FRED series: the CBOE 10-year index on Yahoo (4.944%) and an intraday print reported by Investing.com (around 4.92%).

August 2026 CPI has not been published yet. Every August CPI figure turned up in search this run was a pre-release consensus estimate; BLS's own release page still showed July data at the time this ran, so no August CPI number appears anywhere on this page.

A SEBI probe into a JPMorgan unit in India, reported 9 September, was left out. Coverage was found only through search snippets and paywalled pages that could not be opened directly to confirm the date and figures on the source itself, so it is omitted rather than reported second-hand. The unrelated Jane Street SEBI matter that some of that coverage cites as background remains a 2025 action; nothing found this run dates a new Jane Street development to 2026.

Fed hike odds for 16 September are reported as a range, not a number. Estimates spanning roughly 48% to 70% were in circulation across CME FedWatch, Kalshi, Polymarket and press accounts around this run. Picking one and presenting it as the market's view would be a fabrication dressed as precision.
No trading logic lives here. This page reports what printed and what moved it. It does not size, rank or recommend anything.

instruments.name: S&P 500
instruments.note: Yahoo Finance daily closes. Fourth consecutive down session into 10 Sep, -2.01% over those four days. The index is 2.7% below its 13 Aug close of 7,798.99, the highest in this window. Nothing here is back-filled: 7 Sep is absent because US markets were shut for Labor Day.

instruments.name: US 10-year yield
instruments.note: FRED DGS10, the primary series, which publishes with a lag. Its latest observation is 9 Sep at 4.83%, which is +3.0bp on the session and +4.0bp since 1 Sep. FRED has not yet published 10 Sep. A separate source, the CBOE 10-year yield index on Yahoo, printed 4.944% for 10 Sep against 4.837% the day before, so +10.7bp on its own series. That figure is quoted here, attributed, rather than spliced onto the end of the FRED series: a basis-point move computed across two providers is not a real move. 7 Sep is blank in FRED because the market was shut.

instruments.name: Brent crude
instruments.note: ICE Brent front-month futures settlements from Yahoo Finance. The 9 Sep settle of 101.21 matches the figure Reuters and Al-Monitor reported for that session, so level and percent reconcile against the press. Up 12.6% over five sessions. Note that FRED's DCOILBRENTEU, which is the EIA Europe Brent spot assessment rather than the futures contract, showed 109.51 for 9 Sep; the futures settle is used here because it is what the market traded. Today's session is still open and is not charted: Brent was around 106.04 at 15:05 SGT today, an intraday reading, not a close.

instruments.name: VIX
instruments.note: Up 24.6% over five sessions but still at 17.84. This remains the strongest single argument against reading the selloff as disorderly: a rates-and-oil repricing, not a liquidity event. Above roughly 25 that reading would need revisiting.

instruments.name: Nasdaq Composite
instruments.note: Yahoo Finance daily closes. Down 0.65% on 10 Sep and 1.89% over four sessions. The long-duration end of the equity market is doing more of the work than the headline index, which is what a rates-led move looks like.

instruments.name: Dow Jones Industrial
instruments.note: The 10 Sep close of 52,064.10 is a fall of 316.56 points on the day, which matches the 316.56-point decline reported for the session by CNBC, so the level and the change reconcile against an independent account. No session is missing from this series.

instruments.name: Russell 2000
instruments.note: Small caps have led the decline throughout: -2.60% over four sessions against -2.01% for the S&P 500. Domestic, rate-sensitive and more levered, which fits a rates-driven move rather than a growth scare.

instruments.name: US 2-year yield
instruments.note: FRED DGS2, same lag as the 10-year. 4.43% on 9 Sep: +4.0bp on the session and +26.0bp since 25 Aug. The 2-year is the cleanest read available here on what the market thinks the Fed does on 16 Sep, and it has been rising with the 10-year rather than against it, which says the move is about policy and inflation rather than term premium alone. The 10s2s spread is 0.40 percentage points. FRED DGS20 was 5.28% on the same date.

instruments.name: WTI crude
instruments.note: NYMEX WTI front-month settlements from Yahoo Finance. The 9 Sep settle of 96.05 matches the press figure for that session. Brent's premium to WTI on 10 Sep is 5.15 a barrel. Today is still trading and is not charted.

instruments.name: Nikkei 225
instruments.note: Closes only. Tokyo actually rose 0.20% on 10 Sep; the shock is landing today instead, and today is not on this chart. Japan is the cleanest expression of it: near-total oil import dependence plus a Bank of Japan the market now expects to move on 18 Sep. The intraday reading at 15:05 SGT today was about 64,011.34, roughly -1.9% below the 10 Sep close, but an unsettled session is not a close and is not charted.

instruments.name: Hang Seng
instruments.note: Closes only. Down 1.27% on 10 Sep and 1.03% over five sessions, so most of the damage is recent rather than cumulative. Hong Kong was still open when this ran, so today is omitted rather than shown as a close; the intraday level at 15:05 SGT was about 24,806.26.

instruments.name: Straits Times Index
instruments.note: Singapore closes. Down 0.70% on 10 Sep and 1.01% over five sessions, against 1.03% for the Hang Seng over the same five. Today is omitted because the session was still open; the intraday level at 15:05 SGT was about 5,677.83.

instruments.name: Nvidia, USD per share
instruments.note: Promoted out of the percent chips into a full close series. The unit chip reads index because the feed contract allows only three unit values; these are US dollars per share. Down 2.37% on 10 Sep and 2.70% over five sessions. The AI-complex bellwether: if the selloff were about AI demand rather than the discount rate, this is where it would show first.

news.b: The US military struck and sank five Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island on 9 September; crews were reportedly told to abandon ship before the strikes. Iran retaliated the same day, attacking ten vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, firing roughly twenty ballistic missiles at a US base in Jordan, and claiming strikes on two US Navy destroyers. Brent settled at 107.63 on 10 September, up 6.3% on the day, after wire reports had it briefly trading above 108 intraday; WTI settled at 102.48, up 6.7%. Both figures are the same level and percent change shown in the Brent and WTI series above, from the same Yahoo Finance futures feed.
news.t: US sinks five Iranian tankers, Iran hits back near Hormuz: the war's biggest wave of shipping attacks yet
news.un: Al Jazeera, corroborated by AP wire

news.b: The S&P 500 closed at 7,591.70, down 0.6% and its fourth consecutive decline; the Dow fell 316.56 points to 52,064.10, also down 0.6%; the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.7% to 26,081.72; and the Russell 2000, the session's worst performer, fell 1.0% to 2,890.95. The Associated Press attributed the move to oil returning to levels last seen in May. Small caps have led the decline all week: the Russell is down over 4% across the last four sessions against roughly 2% for the S&P 500, which is what a rates-and-oil repricing looks like rather than a growth scare.
news.t: Fourth straight down session for US equities as oil and yields spike

news.b: The BLS reported final-demand PPI up 0.4% in August and 5.4% over twelve months, above the roughly 5.3% consensus. Core final demand, excluding food, energy and trade services, rose a calmer 0.3% and 4.7% year on year. Final-demand goods rose 1.1% against 0.1% for services, an energy-led split that argues this is an oil shock passing through wholesale prices rather than a broad domestic inflation problem, which is exactly the distinction the Fed has to make before its 16 September decision.
news.t: August PPI +0.4% on the month, 5.4% on the year, and it is almost all energy

news.b: The 10-year Treasury yield reached about 4.92% intraday on 10 September, the highest since November 2023, as the hot PPI print compounded the oil-driven inflation scare. That is an intraday reading, not a close, and is not charted in the yield series above; the chart's 10-year level comes from FRED's constant-maturity series, which had published only through 9 September at 4.83% as of this run. A third, separate reading, the CBOE 10-year yield index on Yahoo, printed 4.944% for 10 September and is quoted, attributed, in that instrument's note rather than spliced onto the FRED series.
news.t: 10-year Treasury yield touches its highest intraday level since November 2023

news.b: Intel -5.6%, Micron -4.9%, AMD -3.4%, Marvell -3.4%, Nvidia -2.4%, Broadcom -1.0% and TSMC -1.7% on the session, while Apple rose 3.6%. Nothing that day questioned AI capex; an intraday 10-year yield near 4.9% simply repriced the longest-duration cash flows in the index. Worth watching rather than trading: if a semis selloff ever arrives with an order-book story attached, that is a different event entirely.
news.t: Semis sold off with the discount rate, not on a demand story

news.b: The FOMC held its target range at 3.50%-3.75% at the 29 July meeting and next meets 15-16 September, with the statement and updated projections due at 2pm ET on the 16th. Governor Waller said on 3 September that his vote would be heavily influenced by the August inflation data, framing a hike as conditional rather than decided. Since then, estimates of a 25bp hike's probability have ranged widely by source: CME FedWatch has shown the high 50s to mid 60s, Kalshi around 48%, Polymarket around 49%, and several accounts cite numbers near 70% after the 10 September PPI and oil move. That is too wide a spread to report as one number, so this item is flagged rather than stated as fact.
news.t: The Fed decides on 16 September and the odds of a hike are genuinely contested

news.b: The HFRI Fund Weighted Composite gained 1.7% in August, reversing a July decline, with roughly 70% of funds posting a positive month. Macro strategies led at 4.1%, and within macro the Commodity index gained 10.0%, its best month since the index's 2008 inception; Systematic Diversified/CTA added 3.45% and Discretionary Thematic 3.4%. Equity Hedge managed 1.5%, Relative Value 0.3% and Event-Driven 0.15%. Dispersion was wide: the top decile of constituent funds averaged 10.3% against -4.9% for the bottom decile, which is a large spread for one month.
news.t: HFR: macro and CTAs ran away with August, best commodity month on record for the index

news.b: SEC Release No. IA-6992, issued 31 August and published in the Federal Register on 3 September, further delays the compliance date for the February 2024 Form PF amendments from 1 October 2026 to 1 July 2027, per the SEC's own rulemaking page. It is the fourth delay tied to that 2024 rulemaking. For private-fund and quant shops the practical effect is roughly nine more months before the more granular exposure, liquidity and risk reporting takes effect.
news.t: SEC and CFTC push the Form PF compliance date out again, to 1 July 2027

news.b: Per Nvidia's 8-K, the company agreed on 2 September to acquire Hugging Face for approximately $11.9bn payable to its stockholders, plus an equity-based retention pool of up to about $1.0bn for employees who join Nvidia. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 subject to regulatory approval. Hugging Face operates the largest hosting platform and community for open-source models, datasets and applications, so the practical effect is that the default distribution point for open model weights now has a chip vendor as its owner.
news.t: Nvidia to acquire Hugging Face for about $11.9bn

news.b: The Justice Department has opened an investigation, reported 9 September, into Nvidia's December-announced deal with AI chip startup Groq, examining whether structuring it as a non-exclusive technology licence plus the hiring of Groq's founder and other executives, rather than an outright merger, was designed to avoid mandatory antitrust reporting. The DOJ has sent Nvidia a request for information; people close to the matter say unwinding the deal is unlikely and a fine is the more probable outcome. The deal's size is reported inconsistently, $17bn in the original New York Times account and $20bn in other outlets' headlines; both are noted here because neither has been independently reconciled. Nvidia's on-record response calls Groq 'the American system working as designed to promote innovation, reward entrepreneurs, and benefit consumers.'
news.t: DOJ examines whether Nvidia's Groq licensing deal was structured to dodge antitrust review
news.un: New York Times reporting, via KFGO wire republish

news.b: Per the deal exhibit filed with the SEC, Analog Devices agreed on 9 September to pay Alif Semiconductor's stockholders $1.35bn in upfront cash plus up to $200m in contingent consideration. Alif makes microcontrollers and fusion processors built for AI workloads at the edge rather than in the data centre; the deal is expected to close before the end of 2026 subject to antitrust clearance. It is a smaller, quieter data point in the same AI-capex story that Nvidia's Hugging Face purchase and the Groq inquiry are part of: silicon vendors buying into every layer of the stack.
news.t: Analog Devices to buy Alif Semiconductor for $1.35bn, eyeing AI-native edge chips

origin: Live feed: Yahoo Finance daily closes + FRED DGS10/DGS2/DGS20

why.t: Oil is the origin, not a symptom
why.b: Brent +12.5% over five sessions to 107.63 and WTI +12.6% to 102.48 — both benchmarks moving together, which is a global supply premium rather than a regional dislocation. Iran struck ten ships near the Strait of Hormuz and the US sank five Iranian tankers; transit has fallen below 2m barrels a day against 8-9m before 30 August. Every other line below is downstream of this one.

why.t: Yields are how it reaches everything else
why.b: The 10-year is 4.83% and the 2-year 4.43% on the latest published observation, +3bp and +4bp on the session, a 0.40 point spread. August PPI ran 5.4% on the year with energy +4.2% and diesel +24.1%. Both ends of the curve rising together says policy and inflation rather than term premium alone. These are FRED series and publish a day or two late; the instrument note carries the more recent market print, attributed.

why.t: Small caps are worst because they are the most rate-exposed
why.b: Russell 2000 -2.60% over four sessions against -2.01% for the S&P 500. Domestic revenue, floating-rate debt and thinner margins mean a funding-cost shock lands on them first. This ordering is the clearest evidence the move is about the discount rate rather than about growth.

why.t: Semis fell on duration, not on demand
why.b: INTC -5.6%, MU -4.9%, AMD -3.4%, NVDA -2.4% on 10 Sep, with nothing in the session questioning AI orders. They hold the longest-dated cash flows in the index, so a higher discount rate marks them down hardest. A semi selloff arriving with an order-book story attached would be a different event entirely.

why.t: Apple rose in the same session, which is the point
why.b: +3.6% on product news while the semis fell. Shorter-duration, cash-generative, less sensitive to the discount rate. The market is discriminating by duration rather than selling equities indiscriminately.

why.t: Japan is the worst-placed market in this shock
why.b: The Nikkei closed +0.20% on its last completed session and is lower again intraday today — see its note, which carries the unsettled reading rather than charting it. Near-total oil import dependence, a 30-year JGB at 4.055%, and a Bank of Japan that 97% of surveyed economists expect to raise to 1.25% on 18 September. The shock hits the currency, the cost base and the policy rate at once.

why.t: The VIX says repricing, not panic
why.b: At 17.84 after +24.6% over five sessions: higher, but nowhere near stressed. This is the strongest single argument against reading the selloff as disorderly. Above roughly 25 that read would need revisiting.
